summary.en: Led by the Beatles, rock musicians began shifting from craftsmen to artists, and an aesthetic centered on authenticity took shape.
summary.zh: 在the Beatles的带领下，摇滚乐人开始实现从匠人到艺术家的转变，同时树立了以真实性为核心的审美观。

body.zh:
现在，我们将通过the Beatles的音乐来考察“从匠人到艺术家”这一理念。当然不只有the Beatles，这种转变也能见诸其他艺人的生涯；不过我们将以the Beatles为范例，因为他们正是个中领军者。

所谓匠人，就是一旦学会特定的技能、能够将其熟练运用后，此人就开始反反复复地运用它。比如，那些以制作桌子为生的人发现了一种方法，不仅能够很好地实现燕尾榫接，而且效率很高、能够助长业绩——这时他们会做什么呢？自此之后，他们会在自己制作的每一张桌子上应用这种工艺元素。他们发现了一种很好的方法，所以他们会一次又一次地应用它。这就是“工艺”的一种常见含义。他们不会说，好吧，既然我已经用那种方法做了一张桌子，那就不该以同样的方法再做一张了，否则我就是在自我重复。这听起来很好笑，对吧？然而再想想艺术家的工作吧，对他们而言，最刻薄的评价莫过于“哦，他不过是将同一首交响曲写了很多遍罢了”或者“她不过是将同一首歌录了很多次罢了”。如果你给出这样的评价，你的意思大致就是，他们不断地重复自己做过的事情，没有一点创意。他们没有做出任何新的东西，这就是一种缺陷。所以，“匠人”就是那些一招鲜吃遍天的人；“艺术家”则会为了创新而不断挣扎，不愿意被批评为只会自我重复的人。这两者有些相互对立的意思。

而我们能从60年代中期的the Beatles和许多其他艺人身上看到的，是一种从匠人到艺术家的转变。对于the Beatles来说，匠人做派就意味着固守在传统美式流行歌的框架中创作。如果你想听听the Beatles的早期作品，那些类似于布里尔大厦 (Brill Building) 模式的东西，1963年的《Please Please Me》和1964年的《I Want to Hold Your Hand》都是很好的例子。这些歌曲都是那种非常典型的模式化作品，个中蕴含了所谓的“Beatles式魅力”等等，但基本上还是布里尔大厦模式的流行歌。虽然如此，到了他们在1964年夏天发表的《A Hard Day's Night》（录制于夏天的几个月前），你能从中看出一些微小的迹象，它们表明乐队正在拓宽原有的界限，寻找更有创造性的创作方法，迈出成为艺术家的第一步。到1965年，由于Bob Dylan的重要影响，你能看到像John在65年写的《Help》、《You've Got to Hide Your Love Away》以及Paul 在64年写的《Yesterday》，它们的歌词显得更加严肃。其实他们在1964年秋天跟Dylan见过一面——提及这个日期，是因为在下节课中我们将看到，1965年夏天之前的Bob Dylan都还不是一个堪称巨星的歌手和表演者。此前他的专辑在民谣圈里颇有名气，但只有圈内人对这些作品才有所了解；而the Beatles很钦佩Dylan，Dylan也跟John和Paul谈过，数人聚在一块，Dylan劝说他们在歌词上多下功夫，不要只是写些我爱你、她爱我、我牵你手和她爱你的吻等等，要深入更加严肃的话题。这种转变的迹象最初见之于1965年发表的专辑《Help》，如上所述，像是标题曲《Help》、《You've Got to Hide Your Love Away》以及《Yesterday》。

流行歌曲作者常用一种曲式，叫做AABA式结构。这种结构可以追溯到很久以前的美国流行音乐。它不是唯一的选择，但很多美国作者都采用了这种结构，比如Cole Porter、George Gershwin、Ira Gershwin和Irving Berlin，也就是叮砰巷（Tin Pan Alley）时期的各路作者。看看the Beatles前四张专辑和随之发行的单曲，其中就应用了大量的AABA式。实际上这是一种默认结构了，不采用它的歌曲反而屈指可数。这种结构的采用率可能达到75%到80%。他们并非无意间采用了AABA式然后再将其反复应用，他们十分了解这种结构，因为他们研究过流行音乐的奥秘。这种反复应用，在我看来，或许还带着一丝骄傲。但随着60年代逐渐铺开，你能看到的是AABA式愈发罕见。他们对于歌词有了更多抱负，各种配器也开始加入到音乐中来。歌曲的结构也开始有了变化，因为他们逐渐摆脱了布里尔大厦式思维、走上更受艺术氛围影响的方向。比如1965年我们能听到《Norwegian Wood》，它听上去不像他们创作过的任何东西。音调上，它与之前的作品完全不同；整首歌都在讲述一个有趣的故事，也是听众首次看到他们将西塔尔琴用作配器。再如1966年Paul创作的《Eleanor Rigby》，它刻画了存在性焦虑 (existential angst) 和疏离感之类的状态。《For No One》，这首与破裂的婚姻有关的歌曲，采用了圆号。这也算是一个“先现音”（anticipation），他将会在66年末、67年初的《Penny Lane》中使用高音小号。 顺带一提，《Eleanor Rigby》还采用了弦乐，它像是《Yesterday》的一种延续，但前者及其弦乐编写都比后者稍微前卫一些。当然还有1966年的专辑《Revolver》的收场曲《Tomorrow Never Knows》， 其中John Lennon念诵着摘自Timothy Learie《The Psychadelic Experience》的歌词，而这些歌词又来自《The Tibetan Book of the Dead》（西藏度亡经）。他们采用了磁带回转（tape loops）的技术，这是其之前从未尝试过的东西。《I Want to Hold Your Hand》与《Tomorrow Never Knows》之间有着巨大的风格差异，而两者仅仅相隔了大概两年或稍长一点的时间。

从《I Want to Hold Your Hand》到《Tomorrow Never Knows》的过程，就是从匠人到艺术家的过程。这就是the Beatles的音乐进化。不过他们并非独行者。在60年代，很多艺人也在做着性质相同的工作。下节课我们会讲到，Brian Wilson的the Beach Boys在冲浪音乐上实现了创新。Bob Dylan在创新，很多模仿the Beatles的乐队亦是如此。但the Beatles是一个典型的例子，他们的经历能告诉我们这种轨迹是如何发展出来的，摇滚音乐人是如何开始把自己视为艺术家而非匠人的。摇滚乐开始发展出了一种新的审美，我们可以称之为摇滚的真实性（authenticity）。它意味着，你要写出自己的歌，歌中得有真正的个性和自己的思想感情。你得在唱片录音里亲自弹奏乐器，不得依赖录音室的乐手；唱片里的那个人得是你自己。写我自己的想法，唱我自己的歌，那就是公认的“真实”。所以到了1966、1967年时，举个例子，有消息曝出the Monkees的唱片里的演奏者其实不是乐队自己，而是职业的录音室乐手，这一下子就成了一件丑闻。它意味着the Monkees的音乐是“不真实的”，意味着他们和音乐产业里的势利匠人没什么区别。但就在几年前，作为音乐真实性的象征之一的乐队the Byrds，发表过一首叫做《Mr. Tambourine Man》的歌曲。唯一参与了演奏的乐队成员是Roger McGuinn，他负责弹12弦吉他。而其他的器乐声，统统来自录音室乐手。那些Beatles的音乐，《Pet Sounds》里的Beach Boys作品，全都是由录音室乐手演奏出来的。不过你也能看到，人们对这种现象的微词越积越多，音乐人就开始亲自演奏唱片里的音乐；若不如此，就会被批为“不真实”。真实性的理念同时意味着，至少你对自己的形象有所把控，你的内在确实和你的模样相吻合。你没有在扮演什么角色，没有戴着什么面具；你是真实、真挚的。这样一种形象设计，不可或缺。

关于the Beatles，我最后还要讲的是：作为艺术家要奋力进步。不要重复自我，要一直往前，那才是你应去的方向。你要一直尝试新的、不同的东西，试着去开拓边界。当然也有种例外，那就是你可以回归根源。你永远可以给音乐做减法、回归自己的根源，因为那也被人视作真实性的一种符号。你不能做的是，一次又一次地复制成功的先例。到了60年代末——进入70年代就更是如此了——几乎人人都以我所概括的真实性的审美观来衡量音乐，至少调频摇滚电台（FM rock）就是这样操作的。然而在60年代的前半段，自50年代结束至65年为止，没有人会这样做。当时流行的仍是布里尔大厦的老一套。而从匠人到艺术家的草根运动不仅见诸the Beatles的音乐，更见诸整个摇滚史。实际上，在接下来几节课里走近1967、1968和1969年时，我会详细讲讲这种整体的运动。我们会讲到调频摇滚电台如何继续发扬真实性至上的态度，而调幅摇滚电台（AM rock）——这就是两类电台分道扬镳的时刻了——仍以布里尔大厦式思维坚守极端的单曲导向。调频电台选择的，是秉持专辑导向的艺人以及真实性的审美观。谈了这么多，接下来就让我们转向英国布鲁斯音乐的兴起，或者说布鲁斯音乐在英国的复兴,以及这种运动如何催生了像the Rolling Stones和the Yardbirds这样的乐队。
body.en:
Now we examine the craftsman-to-artist idea through the Beatles’ music. Of course it appears in other careers too; we use the Beatles as the example because they led the way.

A craftsman, once skilled at a technique and able to use it fluently, applies it again and again. Say people who make tables for a living find a way to cut dovetails well and efficiently—good for business. What do they do? From then on they use that craft element on every table. They found a good method, so they apply it again and again. That is a common sense of “craft.” They do not say: well, since I made one table that way, I must not make another the same way or I am repeating myself. That sounds funny, right? Now think of artists: the harshest criticism is “oh, he just wrote the same symphony many times” or “she just recorded the same song over and over.” That roughly means they keep repeating what they have done, with no invention—nothing new, a flaw. So “craftsman” means those who live off one trick; “artist” means those who struggle to innovate and refuse the charge of mere self-repetition. The two ideas partly oppose each other.

What we see in the mid-1960s Beatles and many other artists is a shift from craftsman to artist. For the Beatles, craftsman practice meant staying inside traditional American pop song frames. If you want early Beatles close to Brill Building models, 1963’s “Please Please Me” and 1964’s “I Want to Hold Your Hand” are good examples—very typical formula pieces, with so-called Beatles charm and so on, but basically Brill Building pop. Even so, by “A Hard Day’s Night” (released summer 1964, recorded months earlier) you hear small signs they are widening the frame, seeking more creative methods—first steps toward being artists. By 1965, under Bob Dylan’s important influence, you get songs like John’s “Help!” and “You’ve Got to Hide Your Love Away,” and Paul’s “Yesterday” (written 1964), with more serious lyrics. They met Dylan in autumn 1964—I note the date because next lecture we will see that before summer 1965 Dylan was not yet a star performer on that scale. His albums were known in folk circles, but mainly to insiders; the Beatles admired him, and Dylan talked with John and Paul, urging them to dig into lyrics—not only I love you, she loves me, hold your hand, and kisses—but more serious subjects. Signs of that shift first show on 1965’s Help!, as above: the title track, “You’ve Got to Hide Your Love Away,” and “Yesterday.”

Pop songwriters often use AABA form, going back a long way in American popular song. Not the only option, but many American writers used it—Cole Porter, George and Ira Gershwin, Irving Berlin, the Tin Pan Alley crowd. Look at the Beatles’ first four albums and related singles: heavy AABA use. It was almost the default; songs that skip it are few—maybe 75% to 80% AABA. They did not stumble into AABA and reuse it by accident; they knew the structure because they had studied how pop works. That reuse, I think, may even carry a touch of pride. But as the 1960s unfold, AABA grows rarer. Ambition in lyrics rises; new instrumentation enters. Song structures change as they leave Brill Building thinking for a more art-driven direction. In 1965 we hear “Norwegian Wood,” unlike anything they had written—tonally different, telling an interesting story, and the first time we see them use sitar as color. In 1966 Paul’s “Eleanor Rigby” sketches existential angst and alienation. “For No One,” about a broken marriage, uses French horn—an anticipation of the piccolo trumpet he will use on “Penny Lane” in late 1966 / early 1967. “Eleanor Rigby” also uses strings, a continuation of “Yesterday,” but a bit more advanced in writing. And the closer of 1966’s Revolver, “Tomorrow Never Knows”: John intones lines from Timothy Leary’s The Psychedelic Experience, themselves drawn from the Tibetan Book of the Dead; they use tape loops, something they had never tried. The stylistic gap between “I Want to Hold Your Hand” and “Tomorrow Never Knows” is huge—and only about two years, or a bit more, separate them.

The path from “I Want to Hold Your Hand” to “Tomorrow Never Knows” is the craftsman-to-artist path. That is the Beatles’ musical evolution. They were not alone. In the 1960s many artists did work of the same kind. Next we will see Brian Wilson’s Beach Boys innovating on surf. Dylan innovates; many Beatles-imitating bands do too. But the Beatles are a clear case of how the trajectory developed—how rock musicians began to see themselves as artists rather than craftsmen. Rock developed a new aesthetic we can call rock authenticity: write your own songs, with real personality and feeling; play the instruments on the record yourself, do not rely on session players; the person on the record must be you. My ideas, my songs—that is the accepted “real.” So by 1966–67, when news broke that the Monkees’ records were played by studio professionals, not the band, it became a scandal—“inauthentic,” no different from industry craftsmen. Yet only a few years earlier the Byrds—later a symbol of authenticity—issued “Mr. Tambourine Man” with only Roger McGuinn of the band playing (12-string); the rest was session players. Beatles records and Beach Boys work on Pet Sounds used session players too. But complaints piled up; musicians began playing their own records or face the charge of being “inauthentic.” Authenticity also meant at least some control of your image—inside matching outside. Not playing a role, not wearing a mask; sincere and real. That kind of image design was indispensable.

One last point on the Beatles: as an artist you push forward. Do not repeat yourself; keep going—that is the direction. Keep trying new and different things; try to open the borders. One exception: you may return to roots. You can always strip music back to your roots; that too is read as a sign of authenticity. What you must not do is copy successful precedents again and again. By the late 1960s—and even more in the 1970s—almost everyone measured music by the authenticity aesthetic I have sketched, at least on FM rock radio. In the first half of the 1960s, from the end of the 1950s to 1965, no one did. Brill Building practice still ruled. The grassroots move from craftsman to artist shows not only in Beatles music but across rock history. In the next few lectures, as we approach 1967–69, I will detail that wider movement. We will see how FM rock radio kept amplifying authenticity-first attitudes, while AM rock—this is when the two paths split—stuck to Brill Building thinking and extreme singles orientation. FM chose album-oriented artists and the authenticity aesthetic. Enough for now: next we turn to the rise of British blues—or the blues revival in Britain—and how that movement helped produce bands like the Rolling Stones and the Yardbirds.
